content: In one placebo-controlled trial, based on a 120-week observation period, a death occurred during the 24 weeks of SIRTURO administration. The cause of the imbalance in deaths remains unexplained. No discernible relationship was observed between death and factors such as sputum culture conversion, relapse, sensitivity to other TB drugs, HIV status, or disease severity. SIRTURO should only be used when no other effective treatment regimen is available. QT Prolongation SIRTURO has been shown to prolong the QT interval. An electrocardiogram (ECG) should be performed prior to initiating treatment and at least at weeks 2, 12, and 24 after starting SIRTURO. Baseline serum potassium, calcium, and magnesium levels should be measured and corrected if abnormal. If QT prolongation is detected, follow-up monitoring of electrolytes is recommended. The following factors may increase the risk of QT prolongation in patients receiving SIRTURO, necessitating close ECG monitoring: Concurrent use of other QT-prolonging drugs, including fluoroquinolones, macrolide antibacterial drugs, and the antimycobacterial drug clofazimine. A history of Torsade de Pointes. A history of congenital long QT syndrome. A history of hypothyroidism or bradyarrhythmias. A history of uncompensated heart failure. Serum calcium, magnesium, or potassium levels below the lower limits of normal. SIRTURO and all other QT-prolonging drugs should be discontinued if the patient develops: Clinically significant ventricular arrhythmia. A QTcF interval exceeding 500 ms, confirmed by repeat ECG. Frequent ECG monitoring is required to confirm that the QTc interval has returned to baseline. If syncope occurs, an ECG should be obtained to assess for QT prolongation. SIRTURO has not been studied in patients with ventricular arrhythmias or recent myocardial infarction. Hepatic-Related Adverse Drug Reactions (ADRs) Hepatic-related adverse drug reactions were reported more frequently with the use of SIRTURO in combination with other TB drugs compared to TB drugs without SIRTURO. Alcohol and other hepatotoxic drugs should be avoided during SIRTURO treatment, particularly in patients with reduced hepatic reserve. Symptoms and laboratory tests (ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin) should be monitored at baseline, monthly during treatment, and as clinically indicated. If serum aminotransferase levels increase to more than three times the upper limit of normal (ULN), repeat testing should be performed within 48 hours. Testing for viral hepatitis should be conducted, and other hepatotoxic medications should be discontinued. Evidence of new or worsening liver dysfunction (e.g., significant elevations in aminotransferases and/or bilirubin, or symptoms such as fatigue, anorexia, nausea, jaundice, dark urine, liver tenderness, or hepatomegaly) should prompt further evaluation by the prescriber. SIRTURO should be discontinued if: Aminotransferase elevations are accompanied by total bilirubin elevation greater than two times the ULN. Aminotransferase elevations exceed eight times the ULN. Aminotransferase elevations persist beyond two weeks. Drug Interactions CYP3A4 Inducers/Inhibitors Bedaquiline, the active ingredient in SIRTURO, is metabolized by CYP3A4. Co-administration with CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., rifampin, rifapentine, rifabutin) may reduce bedaquiline’s systemic exposure and therapeutic effect, and should therefore be avoided during SIRTURO treatment. Co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors may increase systemic exposure to bedaquiline, potentially raising the risk of adverse reactions. The use of strong CYP3A4 inhibitors for more than 14 consecutive days should be avoided unless the benefit of the drug combination outweighs the risk. Appropriate clinical monitoring for SIRTURO-related adverse reactions is recommended. HIV-TB Co-Infected Patients There is no clinical data on the combined use of antiretroviral agents and SIRTURO in HIV/MDR-TB co-infected patients. Limited clinical data exist on the use of SIRTURO in HIV/MDR-TB co-infected patients (n=22) who were not receiving antiretroviral therapy. Treatment Failure SIRTURO should be administered under directly observed therapy (DOT). It should only be used in combination with at least three drugs that are active against the patient’s TB isolate. Isolates from patients who fail to convert or relapse following treatment should be tested for bedaquiline minimum inhibitory concentrations.
